questions.q: What is the Restricted Pod Security Standard designed to enforce?
options: No restrictions at all, for maximum compatibility
Non-root execution, dropped capabilities by default, a required seccomp profile, and no privilege escalation
Only network policy rules, with no restrictions on container privileges
Automatic image vulnerability scanning
questions.explain: Restricted is the strictest of Kubernetes' three built-in Pod Security Standards, enforcing non-root execution, dropped capabilities, a required seccomp profile, and blocking privilege escalation.

questions.q: How are Pod Security Standards typically enforced across many pods at once?
options: By editing every individual pod specification by hand
Via a label applied at the namespace level, such as pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
By rebuilding every container image
They cannot be enforced across multiple pods at once
questions.explain: Applying an enforcement label to a namespace holds every pod inside that namespace to the chosen standard, without needing to configure each pod definition individually.

questions.q: What does setting allowPrivilegeEscalation: false in a securityContext prevent?
options: The container from making any network connections
A process from gaining more privileges than it started with, even through a setuid binary
The container from being scanned for vulnerabilities
The pod from being scheduled on any node
questions.explain: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false blocks a process from escalating its privileges beyond what it started with, closing off a common path to privilege escalation inside the container.

questions.q: Why does a hardened, distroless image from Lesson 20 still need Kubernetes-level security controls?
options: Because distroless images cannot run inside Kubernetes at all
Because nothing about the image itself prevents the cluster from running it as root with every capability enabled, unless the cluster enforces otherwise
Because Kubernetes automatically hardens every image it runs
Because image hardening and cluster security are the exact same control
questions.explain: Image hardening and cluster-level enforcement are separate layers — a well-built image can still be run insecurely if the cluster doesn't enforce restrictions like non-root execution and dropped capabilities.

questions.q: What does dropping ALL Linux capabilities in a securityContext accomplish?
options: It removes every fine-grained kernel permission by default, so nothing beyond what's explicitly added back is available
It deletes the container image from the registry
It disables all networking for the pod
It automatically patches any vulnerable library in the image
questions.explain: Dropping all capabilities starts the container with none of the fine-grained Linux kernel permissions beyond basic process execution — any specific capability actually needed must be added back explicitly.
